On the meaning of "bi-qadar", Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari mention a prior divine decree in one view and sufficiency for good in another. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi report differing readings of "tukhrajun" without preferring one. Al-Tabari, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take "anshharna" to mean "we revived". Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir read "al-azwaj" as kinds and species, al-Hasan as night and day, heaven and earth, while al-Razi takes it to mean everything that is paired. The commentators also quote the words recommended when mounting a beast or a ship, such as "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us".

This verse names two of God's blessings upon people: He created all kinds of pairs, and He made for you, among ships and livestock, what you ride. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that the 'pairs' are kinds and types of all things, that al-fulk means ships, and that the livestock are mainly camels, although Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi also include cattle. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that the word 'min' is partitive, since only some animals are ridden, and that mules, horses and donkeys are also included in what is ridden. The pronoun in 'upon its backs' refers to 'what', and most commentators understand that the purpose is to sit comfortably on the backs of these means of transport, to remember God's favour and to praise Him in heart and tongue. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report recitations said upon mounting, such as 'Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us', along with supplications attributed to the Prophet and to Ali. The word 'muqrinin' is explained by most as 'able to master it', though some take it as 'equal in strength' or 'in control'. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi add that the verse ends by recalling the return to God, a reminder of resurrection. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur stress the lesson of gratitude and of recognising human weakness before the power of the mounts.

The commentators explain that the verse recounts God's favours in providing ships and livestock, on which people can settle on land and at sea. The verse asks the rider to remember his Lord's blessing when he mounts, to be grateful in his heart and then to say aloud: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could never have controlled it." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take "muqrinin" to mean "able to control", al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubayda take it to mean "mastering", and Qatada to mean "equal in strength". All agree that the closing words "and to our Lord we shall indeed return" affirm the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi note that the rider faces danger at sea or from a fall, which is why the thought of returning to God is recalled. The scholars differ on the "li" of "li-tastawu": most read it as purpose, Ibn 'Atiyya as an imperative, and Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin as a lam of consequence. On the pronoun in "dhuhurihi", al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it to refer to "what you ride", with the plural "dhuhur" following the meaning, as al-Farra' explains by comparing the word to an army. Many commentators cite reports of a supplication for mounting, among them one attributed to 'Ali, though Ibn Kathir notes that some of its transmitters are weak.

This verse calls the rider of a mount or a ship to remember God's favour in making these vehicles subservient to him, and to say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could not have controlled it ourselves; and to our Lord we will surely return." The commentators agree that "al-fulk" (ships) and "al-an'am" (grazing animals, mainly camels) refer to means of transport on land and sea, and that the lam in "li-tastawu" expresses purpose or outcome. The pronoun in "zuhurihi" refers back to "ma", which explains the plural "backs" alongside the singular pronoun, as al-Tabari, al-Farra' and Ibn 'Atiyya note. On the meaning of "muqrinin", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Abbas take it as "able to control", Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash as "subduing", while Qatada and al-Baghawi mention being equal in strength. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur see the mention of returning to God as a reminder of the danger of travel, urging the rider to prepare for death, and Ibn 'Ashur also reads it as an affirmation of resurrection. On the identity of the animals, Sa'id ibn Jubayr includes cattle and camels, whereas Mu'adh, whose view al-Qurtubi finds sound, limits it to camels. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, cite hadiths describing the Prophet's supplications when mounting, and they treat this remembrance as recommended.

This verse describes those who assigned to God a share of His servants, claiming the angels are His daughters, and it condemns them as manifestly ungrateful. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the word juz' as offspring, specifically daughters, and link the verse to what follows, where God rebukes them for assigning daughters to Him while keeping sons for themselves, and for darkening with shame when a daughter is announced to them. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy record other meanings, such as equal, peer or associate, which Qatada applies to idols and Pharaoh. Some philologists explained the word as meaning daughters, citing verses that al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi regard as forged or doubtful. Several commentators, including al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti, point to the inconsistency of people who acknowledge God as Creator yet ascribe offspring to Him. Al-Shinqiti holds that juz' means son, with the daughters singled out afterwards. On the meaning of mubin, most read it as ingratitude that is plainly evident. Ibn Sa'di stresses the absurdity: a child is part of its parent, while God is utterly unlike His creation.

In this verse God rebukes the idolaters who claimed that the angels are God's daughters. The commentators explain that the word "juz'" means a part or offspring, and that the verb "made" here means attributed or pronounced. Their claim is therefore seen as plain disbelief. God asks a question of reproach: has He taken for Himself daughters, which you yourselves dislike, while choosing for you the sons? The exegetes note that these people attribute to God what they abhor for themselves: when one of them is told of the birth of a daughter, his face darkens with anger and grief. Nearly all agree that the phrase "one raised among ornaments" refers to women, who adorn themselves to make up for their deficiency, and to their weakness in argument, as Qatada reports. Readers and exegetes differ on the reading of "yunashsha'u" and on the grammar of "man". Al-Zamakhshari notes that some philologists take "juz'" to mean female, but he considers the verses cited as fabricated, as al-Zajjaj does. Ibn Kathir stresses that "servants of the Merciful" honours the angels, while the reading "near the Merciful" expresses their nearness. Several commentators finally point out that the polytheists appealed to God's will; God replies that they have no knowledge of this, that they merely guess, and that no revealed book teaches it, so they keep to the imitation of their forefathers.

This verse describes the pagans who attributed daughters to God, even though they themselves strongly disliked daughters: when one of them is told of the birth of a girl, his face darkens and he is filled with grief and rage. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "what he sets up as a likeness to the Most Merciful" refers to ascribing to God an offspring like the creatures, since a child resembles its father. The commentators broadly agree that the verse is a rebuke: how can they attribute to God what they reject for themselves, and assign Him the lesser while keeping the greater for themselves.

They differ on what "his face became dark" means. Al-Mawardi suggests it refers either to the collapse of their comparison or to the news of the girl, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take "zalla" to mean "became." For "kazim," Qatada says grieved, Ikrima distressed, Ibn Abi Hatim silent, and Ibn Zayd full of rage. As for the one "raised in ornament," most read it as the woman, weak in argument according to Qatada and Ibn Kathir, while Ibn Zayd applies it to the idols adorned with gold and silver.

Scholars also weigh several readings: "'ibad al-Rahman" or "'inda al-Rahman," the vocalization of "yunasha'u," and the sense of "juz'," which some take as child, others as portion or equal. Al-Zamakhshari rejects the claim that "juz'" means "girl" in Arabic, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi report it.

This verse condemns those who attribute to God someone who is raised in ornaments and cannot clearly argue in a dispute. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take it to refer to daughters, who are brought up in finery and, being weak, cannot make their case clearly. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi add that adornment with jewellery is permitted for women, while Ibn Sa'di and al-Tabari stress their natural weakness. Ibn Zayd holds that the verse refers to idols, which were decked with gold and silver yet stayed silent, so that "not clear" means they do not answer. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also record the variant readings of the word yunasha'u, whose meanings, to be raised or to grow up, are close. Al-Zamakhshari and others stress the tone of rebuke and mockery. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguish the general rule from exceptions, citing women of sound judgment such as the Queen of Sheba. The broader point is that God is free of any offspring, and that attributing to Him what they dislike for themselves is baseless.

This verse rebukes those who described the angels as female, claiming they are God's daughters, although the angels are the honoured servants of the Most Merciful. The commentators agree that it is a rebuke and a warning: these people spoke without knowledge, since they were not present at the creation of the angels to judge their sex. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see this as a falsehood and grave ignorance about God, and they note that their false testimony will be recorded and that they will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection. On the readings, the transmitters differ between 'ibad (servants) and 'inda (in the presence of). Al-Tabari considers both correct in meaning, while al-Nahhas and Ibn Abi Hatim prefer 'inda for its sense of nearness and rank, and Abu 'Ubayd prefers 'ibad because it more firmly denies that the angels are God's offspring. As for ashahidu, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir read it as a reproachful question, while al-Tabari accepts it under either reading. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi transmit a report that the Prophet asked them how they knew the angels were female, and they answered that they had heard it from their fathers, but Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi regard that report as weak. Ibn Sa'di notes the contradiction in their view, since the same people consider daughters inferior yet attribute them to God.

This verse reports the claim of the polytheists, mainly the Quraysh, who said: had the Most Merciful willed it, we would not have worshipped these idols or angels, meaning that their worship is approved by God, for otherwise He would have punished them. Mujahid and Ibn Juraij take the pronoun to refer to the idols, while Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi take it to refer to the angels they called daughters of God. The commentators agree that God rejects this claim: they have no knowledge of it and are merely guessing and lying. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that divine will does not mean approval, and that invoking predestination here is an invalid argument. Al-Zamakhshari observes that it is a true statement used for a false purpose, and that it expresses mockery or stubbornness. Al-Razi gives several rational refutations, and Ibn 'Ashur explains that the Arabs confused creative will with legislative command. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya stress that they possess no earlier revealed Book supporting their belief, and that they follow their ancestors blindly. The commentators agree in rejecting the argument, but differ over what the pronoun refers to and over the precise meaning of divine will.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to God's reply to the polytheists who claimed that if the Merciful disapproved of their worship, He would have prevented it. God shows that their claim rests on guesswork and not on knowledge. The question "Or have We given them a Book before this, to which they hold fast?" is a rhetorical denial that they possess any earlier scripture authorising their practice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take the phrase "before it" to refer to the Quran, while al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi allow that it may refer to the Messenger or to their claim. To hold fast means to adhere to the book, act by it and argue from it. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse rules out the appeal to transmitted proof once the rational argument has failed. The same passage mentions the appeal to the fathers, which al-Razi regards as a fault shared by the wrong and the right alike. Most read "umma" as way or religion, and some cite the reading "imma" meaning blessing. Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that no book was sent to the Arabs before the Quran.

This verse reports that the idolaters, having no knowledge or revealed book to rely on, fell back on the claim that they had found their forefathers following a certain community or religion (ummah) and were guided by walking in their footsteps. Most commentators take ummah to mean religion, creed or path. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read it this way, and al-Tabari holds the reading with a damma to be the agreed one. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the reading with a kasra, imma, may mean a path intended or, according to some, a blessing, citing verses by 'Adi ibn Zayd. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take the verse as a condemnation of blind imitation in matters of belief, and al-Razi links this to the wealthy who love comfort and shun the effort of reasoning. Muqatil says the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, 'Utba and Shayba. Several commentators observe that the same reply was given to earlier prophets, which serves as consolation for the Prophet.

This verse shows that the idolaters of Mecca were not the first to speak this way: the wealthy leaders of every town that received a warner said the same, holding to the religion of their fathers without proof. The commentators agree that "ummah" here means path, religion or creed, and that "mutrafuha" refers to the affluent and leading men whom comfort has made arrogant, who love only pleasures and shun the burdens of religion, as az-Zamakhshari and an-Nasafi note. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada understand the imitation (iqtida') as following the fathers in their conduct. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of ummah, namely religion, creed, direction, rectitude and path, and reports that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Mujahid read "imma" with a kasra, a reading taken either as path or as blessing. Ibn Atiyya judges that the sense of blessing fits the argument of the disbelievers, who saw in God's respite a sign of His approval.

The commentators agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ: the messengers before him met the same rejection, and blind adherence to tradition is an ancient error. Al-Razi concludes that imitation, shared by the right and the wrong alike, cannot lead to truth, and that love of ease is its driving force. Ibn Ashur observes that singling out the affluent points to the pride of those who forget their need of God. Ibn Uthaymin specifies that imitation is blameworthy when it concerns error, but permitted out of necessity for someone unable to reason for himself. The readings differ: Ibn Amir and Hafs read "qala" in the narrative form, while most read "qul" as an imperative, and in both cases the Prophet's answer is that even if he brings a path more guided than that of their fathers, they will reject what he brings.

This verse records the messenger speaking to his people who follow their fathers: "Even if I brought you a guidance better than what you found your fathers upon, would you still follow them?" Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the question as a rebuke, and the people's reply as a flat declaration of disbelief in what was sent. The readings differ on the verb: most read "qul" as a command to the Prophet, while Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "qala" in the past tense, referring to the warner. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take both readings as a report of what passed between the messengers and their peoples. On the word "umma", the commentators agree on religion or path, though Mujahid, Qutrub and al-Farra' also give senses such as direction, uprightness or blessing, depending on the vowel. Al-Razi notes that the verse condemns blind imitation, since it is shared by both sides of any dispute. Ibn 'Ashur reads the question as an invitation to reflect, and Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that comparing with a "more guided" path does not concede that the fathers' path was right. The verse closes by recalling the punishment of earlier peoples who rejected their prophets. Al-Tabari cites Qatada's account of sinking and drowning, while other commentators stress the lesson drawn from those nations' fate.

This verse states that God punished the peoples who denied their messengers, and it tells the reader to look at the final outcome of those who denied. The commentators explain that the punishment (intiqam) was a complete destruction, as al-Samʿani and the author of the Jalalayn explain, or a chastisement by famine, killing, captivity and exile, as Abu Hayyan and Ibn ʿAtiyya explain. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, adds that it was a sinking into the earth and drowning, followed by being sent into the Fire, while Ibn Kathir describes the outcome as ruin and perishing. The verse closes a passage in which the unbelievers say, as their predecessors did, that they found their fathers on a religion and will follow their footsteps. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of the word umma, such as religion according to Qatada, path according to Umar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, and others. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAshur stress that this is blind imitation with no support from reason or revelation. Ibn Saʿdi and Ibn ʿUthaymin see in the verse a warning to the contemporaries of the Prophet. The readings differ between qul, the imperative addressed to the Prophet according to most readers, and qala, the past tense referring to the warner, as recited by Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs. Ibn Juzayy considers the first reading the clearer one. The commentators agree that the threat is aimed at the Quraysh and that it urges them to fear the same fate.

The verse records Ibrahim's words to his father and people: he disavows what they worship, except the One who created him, who he trusts will guide him. The commentators agree on the core meaning, the rejection of idolatry. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur note that Quraysh claimed descent from Ibrahim, which gives the reminder the force of a rebuttal. The word baraa', a verbal noun used as an adjective, stays unchanged in number and gender according to al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi note that it can also be read bari'.

The main difference concerns the lasting word Ibrahim left among his descendants. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Sudi and Ibn Kathir take it to be the testimony that there is no god but God, which never ceased to be said by some of his offspring. Ibn Zayd identifies it with submission to God, islam, citing other verses. The meaning of 'aqib is also disputed: for Mujahid and Ibn Abbas it is the progeny, for al-Sudi the family of the Prophet, and for Ibn Shihab children and grandchildren. As for la'allahum yarji'un, opinions range from repentance and remembrance to a return to the truth or to Ibrahim's religion.

Al-Razi and al-Qasimi draw from this passage an argument against blind imitation of ancestors, while Ibn Kathir links it to the wider context of wealth and reward in the hereafter.

This verse reports that Abraham declared his disavowal of what his father and people worshipped, excepting the One who created him, and he confidently stated that this One would guide him. The commentators see in it a reaffirmation of trust in God and a reminder to his people that guidance comes from Him alone. They differ on the nature of the exception: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi treat it as disconnected ("but the One who created me"), while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi allow a connected exception if the idolaters also worshipped God alongside their idols. On the future form "sayahdin", Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur take the sin as emphatic and expressing continuity, a reading that the present-tense parallel in Surat al-Shu'ara' supports, while others read it as a further guidance yet to come.

In the following verse, most exegetes, including Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify the "lasting word" left among his descendants as the profession of divine unity, "There is no god but God". Ibn Zayd takes it to be submission to God, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi link it to Abraham's testament to his sons. The word "'aqib" denotes descendants. As for "perhaps they will return", al-Tabari explains it as repentance and a return to obedience, while al-Farra' takes it as a return to the religion of Abraham.

The wider context concerns the Quraysh's objection that the Quran should have been sent to a great man of Mecca or Ta'if. God replies that mercy is not in their hands, that He apportions their livelihoods and raises some above others so that they may employ one another, and that your Lord's mercy is better than what they amass.

This verse tells that Abraham, peace be upon him, declared his disavowal of his father, his people and what they worshipped, excepting the One who created him, and trusted that He would guide him. He then made the word of monotheism remain among his descendants, hoping that those who had associated partners would return to it. The commentators agree that this word is tawhid. Mujahid and Qatada identify it as the declaration that there is no god but God, Ibn Zayd as Islam, and al-Qurzi as the charge Abraham left to his sons.

They differ on the pronoun in "He made it". Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and most exegetes refer it to Abraham, while al-Zamakhshari and others refer it to God. The word "descendants" (aqib) is understood by Mujahid and Ibn Shihab as children and grandchildren, by al-Suddi as the family of Muhammad, and by Ibn Abbas as successors.

As for "so that they may return", Ibn Abbas and Qatada explain it as repentance and remembrance, al-Nakha'i as a return to the truth, and al-Farra' as a return to Abraham's religion. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect this hope to the Quraysh, whereas Ibn Juzayy sees it as addressed to the descendants who associated partners. Al-Razi draws from the verse that following evidence is better than blind imitation of forefathers.

This verse says that God did not punish the polytheists at once, but gave them and their fathers long life and provision until the Truth came, namely the Qur'an, together with a clear Messenger. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify the Truth as the Qur'an, and take the Clear Messenger to be Muhammad, who explained the laws and proofs to them. Al-Dahhak, however, understood the Truth as Islam. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi connect the verse to what precedes it: Abraham had left the word of monotheism among his descendants in the hope that they would return to it, but the Qurayshites were distracted by comfort and pleasure, so that hope was not fulfilled. Al-Zamakhshari notes that reading the verb in the first person, as God's own speech, serves to rebuke the polytheists more sharply, since a person given many favours ought to be grateful for them. The commentators agree that the disbelievers' response, calling the Qur'an sorcery and rejecting it, shows stubborn denial. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the respite had been granted until a guidance came, and that the Qur'an's arrival ended it, while al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that the Messenger's clarity was complete.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the reaction of the Quraysh when the truth came to them: they called it sorcery and declared their disbelief. Al-Sudi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the pronoun "them" to refer to the Quraysh, so the meaning is that they did not come to their senses after being granted respite and blessings, but persisted in stubbornness. Most of them, including at-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, identify "the truth" with the Quran, while ad-Dahhak takes it to mean Islam. Calling it "sorcery" means that the Quran was described as a magic that bewitches people, and "we disbelieve in it" means that they reject and deny it, as at-Tabari and az-Zamakhshari explain. Ibn 'Atiyya says the accusation of magic was based on the fact that the Quran separates a person from his child or spouse, which is why they likened it to sorcery. Az-Zamakhshari notes that their earlier heedlessness had turned, once the truth arrived, into deliberate opposition, rejection of God's Book and contempt for the Messenger. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse an expression of astonishment at their conduct. The commentators thus agree on the sense of rejection and denial, while differing on the identity of the truth referred to and on the details of the accusation.

The commentators explain that the Quraysh, objecting to the Qur'an, asked why it had not been sent down to a great man from one of the two towns, Mecca or Ta'if. The word 'great' refers to a man of wealth, rank and standing among his people. They differ on who these two men were. Ibn 'Abbas names al-Walid ibn al-Mughira of Mecca and Habib ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi of Ta'if; Mujahid names 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and Ibn 'Abd Yalil; Qatada names al-Walid and 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi; al-Suddi gives another pair. Al-Tabari judged that no clear evidence identifies them, so the verse should be taken in its general sense. God's reply is framed as a question: do they distribute your Lord's mercy? It is God who divided their livelihood in this world and raised some above others in degrees, so that they might employ one another. The commentators broadly agree that the mercy at the end of the verse is greater than wealth, though they differ on what it is: prophethood or Paradise according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, guidance and faith according to others. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir stress that this world is worth little in God's sight, and that true greatness is measured by Him, not by people. On the word sukhriyyan, most read it as employment and service, while some understand possession or mockery.

This verse answers the Quraysh who objected that the Quran was not sent down to a great man of Mecca or Ta'if rather than to Muhammad. God asks whether they are the ones who distribute His mercy, then reminds them that He Himself divided their livelihood in this world, raising some above others in rank so that they may employ one another. The commentators agree that this inequality is a divine wisdom that sustains cooperation and social life. On the meaning of 'mercy', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya take it to mean prophethood, while Qatada and al-Suddi take it to mean Paradise; Ibn Abbas holds that prophethood is better than wealth, and al-Razi also mentions faith and guidance as better than riches. As for the two towns and the two men, Ibn Abbas names al-Walid ibn al-Mughira of Mecca, Mujahid names Utba ibn Rabi'a, and Qatada names Urwa ibn Mas'ud of Ta'if; al-Tabari concludes that no evidence settles the question. On the word 'sukhriyyan', Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi understand it as service and paid employment, Qatada and al-Dahhak as ownership or enslavement, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya as mutual assistance, while a few read it as mockery, a sense most find remote from the context. Finally, Paradise is described as better than the wealth people accumulate in this world.

The commentators explain that this verse stresses how little worldly goods are worth in God's sight. Its meaning is that, were it not that people would all unite in disbelief out of attachment to this world, God would have given the disbelievers silver roofs for their houses, silver stairways by which they climb to their upper rooms, silver doors and couches on which they recline, and gold adornments. All of this is merely the passing enjoyment of the life of this world, while the Hereafter belongs to the righteous with their Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that 'one community' means people united in disbelief. Ibn Zayd adds that it means preferring this world to religion. Al-Hasan, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith that were this world worth a gnat's wing to God, He would not give a disbeliever a drink of water. For al-Tabari and most scholars, 'ma'arij' are staircases; Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' explain the readings of 'suquf' as plurals of 'saqf' or 'saqifa'. Grammarians differ over the reading of 'lamma': Hafs, 'Asim and Hamza read it as 'except', while the majority read it as the lightened particle. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also note that 'zukhruf' is taken by some to mean gold and by others any adornment. The passage answers the Meccans' objection that the Quran should have been sent to a great man of one of the two cities: God replies that wealth and rank do not confer worth in His sight.

The verse 'And for their houses, doors and couches on which they recline' is explained by the commentators as Allah giving disbelievers doors and couches of silver. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, citing Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, state that these are of silver. For 'adornment' (zukhruf), most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi, take it to mean gold, while Ibn Zayd understands furnishings and rugs, and al-Hasan carved decorations. Al-Razi reads it more broadly as ornament. The general sense, shared by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, is that were it not that all people would become disbelievers, Allah would have given these riches to the disbelievers, since worldly things are worthless in His sight. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari cite the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd: 'If this world weighed with Allah the wing of a mosquito, He would not give a disbeliever a drink of water from it.' Ibn Zayd reads the clause as people preferring worldly gain to religion. All agree that these are the enjoyments of the worldly life, while the Hereafter is reserved for the God-fearing. Readers differ on 'lamma', read with shadda as 'except' or without it.

This part of the verse states that the adornments just described, silver roofs, stairways, doors and couches, along with gold ornament, are only a passing enjoyment of the worldly life, while the Hereafter is with your Lord for the God-fearing. The commentators relate this passage to the answer given to those who ranked people by wealth and status. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take zukhruf here to mean gold, Ibn Zayd understands it as household furnishings and carpets, al-Hasan as decorative engravings, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take it as general adornment, with al-Razi still giving gold as the first meaning. On the overall sense, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi explain that had God not feared that all people would unite in disbelief, He would have lavished such wealth on the unbelievers, but He withheld it because this world is worthless in His sight. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, cite the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd: 'If this world weighed as much as a mosquito's wing with God, He would not give a disbeliever a single sip of water', to illustrate its insignificance. The readings differ: 'saqfan' in the singular or 'suqufan' in the plural, and 'lamma' either light or heavy; with the light reading 'in' is the lightened form of 'inna' and 'ma' is superfluous, while with the heavy reading 'in' is negative and 'lamma' means 'except'. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi set out these options without choosing between them. All agree that the Hereafter means Paradise and its lasting delights reserved for the pious, Ibn Kathir specifying those who guard against polytheism and sins, and al-Tabari those who fear God's punishment and obey Him.

The commentators explain that whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, that is the Qur'an and its admonitions, and neither fears His punishment nor hopes for His reward, is given by God a devil who accompanies him, misleads him and makes falsehood seem attractive. They differ on the meaning of the verb ya'shu: Qatada, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba take it to mean turning away, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd read it as going blind, and Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash as the eye being darkened. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes the two readings: one describes a person whose sight is impaired, the other someone who pretends not to see what he knows to be true. As for nuqayyid, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari understand it as 'We assign to him a devil', while al-Mawardi offers 'We cast him as a devil' or 'We substitute one for him'. Nearly all agree that the companion stays with his charge in this world. Ibn Kathir and others report that on the Day of Resurrection the disbeliever is chained to a devil until God casts them both into the Fire, a view that al-Mawardi also transmits from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The commentators agree that the devils block their followers from the right path while making them believe they are rightly guided. At the final encounter, the disbeliever wishes that the distance between himself and his companion were that of the two easts. On the meaning of these two easts, most take it as the east and the west, one term having been used for both; Muqatil and al-Farra' mention the summer and winter risings, and others the sunrise on the longest and shortest days. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that in this world sharing a calamity usually brings comfort, as al-Khansa' said. In the hereafter this comfort is absent, since each is absorbed in his own torment, as al-Razi stresses. The exegetes conclude that these verses console the Prophet, reminding him that guiding the deaf and the blind is not his to do.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the one who turns away from the remembrance of the All-Merciful, that is the Qur'an and the truth it contains, pretending not to see and blinding himself to its light. God then assigns him a devil who never leaves his side. Opinions differ on the verb "ya'shu": according to Qatada and one report from Ibn 'Abbas it means turning away, according to others it means becoming blind or having dimmed sight, and al-Zajjaj, al-Farra' and al-Azhari distinguish "'asha 'an" (to turn away) from "'asha ila" (to head toward something guided by its light). For the reading with a fatha, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima take it to mean blindness. The word "nuqayyid" is understood by most exegetes as God assigning him a devil, while al-Zamakhshari, reading it through his Mu'tazili outlook, takes it as God forsaking him and leaving him to the devils.

The commentators agree that the devils block the disbelievers from the right path while the disbelievers think themselves rightly guided. Some explain the plural pronouns by the collective sense of "man". Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the devil accompanies his companion into the Fire, and that on the Day of Resurrection the disbeliever says, "Would that there were between you and me the distance of the two easts!" Scholars differ on "al-mashriqayn": al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi take it as the east and the west, one term standing for both, as in "al-qamarani"; Muqatil takes it as the summer and winter risings; Ibn Kathir takes it as the distance between east and west. On "lan yanfa'akum", the majority reading makes the shared punishment the subject of the verb, and shared suffering brings no relief, which Razi and al-Baydawi link to the consolation that shared misfortune brings in this world, the theme of al-Khansa's elegy for her brother.

This verse describes the fate of one who turns away from the remembrance of the All-Merciful, which most commentators take to mean the Qur'an. God assigns him a devil who stays with him and bars him from the right path, while he thinks he is rightly guided. On the Day of Resurrection he wishes that the distance between him and his companion were that between the two easts, and he bitterly reproaches him. The commentators agree that the devil blocks the way and that the one who turns away does not perceive his error. As to the meaning of the verb ya'shu, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas render it as turning away, while others say blindness or weak sight. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes the reading with a damma, meaning to feign ignorance of a known truth, from the reading with a fatha, meaning to be blind. Regarding al-mashriqayn, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand it as a figure of speech in which the east stands for both east and west, as in al-qamarayn or al-'umarayn. Others, such as al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, take it to mean the sunrise of winter and of summer. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the singular, the rest the dual, and al-Tabari considers the two readings close in meaning. Several, including al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, report that the disbeliever is chained to his devil until the Fire, a report transmitted from Sa'id al-Jurayri. The commentators agree that sharing the punishment does not lessen it, unlike sharing a calamity in this world, and Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi cite al-Khansa's verses on this point. For the phrase 'and it is indeed a reminder for you and your people', Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand honour, while Ibn Kathir also mentions the interpretation of a reminder. The commentators draw from the passage a warning against bad companions.

This verse explains that whoever turns away from the remembrance of the All-Merciful, meaning the Qur'an and its reminders, is given by God a devil who becomes his inseparable companion, turns him from the straight path, and convinces him that he is rightly guided. The scene then moves to the Day of Judgment, where the disbeliever wishes that the distance between him and his companion were that between the two easts, and is told that sharing the punishment will not benefit them. The commentators agree that the verb ya'shu means to turn away from or become blind to the truth, that the devil is a companion attached to the misguided person, and that associating partners with God in this world is the wrongdoing meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand al-mashriqayn as east and west, one term being used for the pair by a common device of language, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also record the reading of the winter and summer risings. Readers differ on jā'anā, read in the singular for the disbeliever alone or in the dual for him and his devil. Az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss whether annakum is the subject of the verb or a causal clause, depending on the reading. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, note that shared affliction brings consolation in this world, as al-Khansa said, but that this comfort is denied in the hereafter. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the devil is bound to the disbeliever at his resurrection.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet ﷺ with a rhetorical question expressing reproach and wonder: can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, or those who are in clear error? The plain meaning is that making people hear and truly guiding them belongs to God alone, while the Prophet's duty is only to convey the message. The commentators see in the verse a consolation for the Prophet, who was deeply anxious about his people's faith. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the deaf and blind are the unbelievers of Quraysh, who gain nothing from the proofs, and that all this rests with God, who turns hearts as He wills. Al-Zamakhshari reads the question as a wonder at the idea that the Prophet could guide them by compulsion. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi stress that the verse contains a threat against the disbelievers. On the following verses there is a division: al-Tabari and most scholars hold that the threat concerns the Quraysh, who were punished at Badr, whereas al-Hasan and Qatada say it concerns the Muslim community after the Prophet's death, God having spared him the sight of those trials. Ibn 'Ashur reads the question as a denial that the Prophet can reach hardened hearts. The verse also teaches that whoever turns away from the remembrance is given a devil as a companion, and that guidance benefits only those whom God grants it.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage consoling the Prophet ﷺ over the rejection of the Quraysh. God tells him that guidance is not in his hands, that those who turn away from the Remembrance are deaf and blind in clear error, and He promises them retribution. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, hold that the target is the polytheists of Mecca, so that 'if We take you away' means removing you from Mecca or taking your soul before the punishment, and God showed him this at Badr, as Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi say. Al-Hasan and Qatada hold instead that it concerns the believers of his community, and that God spared the Prophet from seeing the calamities that would befall his people after him, a report they cite. Al-Tabari prefers the first view because the verse follows the account of the polytheists, while Ibn Ashur notes that the punishment may come during his lifetime or after his death. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy regard 'ma' as an emphatic particle, and the verse as a threat to the unbelievers in this world or the next. The next verse orders the Prophet to hold fast to the revelation, which is the straight path, and calls the Qur'an an honour for him and his people, for which they will be questioned. Regarding the final part, most report that the questioning is directed at the followers of earlier messengers rather than the messengers themselves, to show that monotheism was the religion of all the prophets.

The commentators explain that this verse continues the address to the Prophet ﷺ about the disbelievers who neither hear nor see the truth, so that guiding them is not his task; he is only to convey the message. God then tells him that if He takes him before the punishment strikes them, they will still be requited, or if He lets him see the promised punishment in his lifetime, God is fully able to bring it upon them. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, hold that the target is the Quraysh, and that this was fulfilled at Badr. Al-Hasan and Qatada, however, take it to concern the Muslim community and the strife after the Prophet's death, God having spared him from seeing it in his lifetime. Al-Sudi understands the promise as victory and dominance over them. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the particle ma functions like an oath and brings the emphatic nun. Al-Tabari judges the first reading to be the more correct, since the context concerns the polytheists. The following verses command the Prophet to hold fast to what has been revealed to him, for he is on a straight path, and state that the Quran is an honour for him and his people. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir add that all earlier messengers called to the worship of God alone, and that the question to be asked concerns their communities or scriptures. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report that some early scholars understood the people to be the Arabs and cited hadiths about Quraysh's standing.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to hold firmly to the Quran revealed to him, for he is on a straight path, a clear road without crookedness, which the commentators, following al-Tabari and Qatada, identify as Islam. The exegetes see in the verse a consolation and a strengthening of the Prophet in the face of his people's rejection. Most agree that the Quran is an honour for the Prophet and his people: Ibn Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the people to be the Quraysh in particular, Mujahid holds that they are the Arabs since the Quran came in their language, while al-Hasan takes them to be the whole community of the Prophet. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi also note that the word dhikr can mean reminder and admonition. As for the words "you will be questioned", Ibn Abbas and Ibn Atiyya explain it as being questioned about the commands and prohibitions of the Quran, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir as being questioned about thankfulness for this blessing and about acting on the book, and Muqatil as being questioned about gratitude. Al-Qurtubi cites a report that leadership belongs to the Quraysh, without settling the matter between the views. Several commentators also read the end of the passage as an announcement that God will ask earlier peoples, and in particular the believers among the People of the Book, whether their prophets ever called to worshipping other gods than God.

This verse states that the Quran is a great honour for the Prophet ﷺ and for his people, and that people will be questioned on the Day of Judgment about how they upheld it. Commentators differ on who "your people" are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Sudi see them first as the Quraysh and then the Arabs in general, since the Quran was revealed in their language and through one of their own; Ibn 'Abbas adds that the Prophet, when asked who would rule after him, would answer "the Quraysh" once this verse was revealed. Qatada extends the term to all who follow him, and al-Hasan to his whole community. On the word "dhikr", most take it to mean honour and nobility, while al-Hasan and others understand a reminder and an admonition; Ibn 'Ashur holds that the word can carry both senses. As for the question, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to concern gratitude for this blessing, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Abbas take it to concern acting on the Quran, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes both readings. The next verse, "ask those whom We sent before you", is read differently: Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it to mean the People of the Book who believed, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand a call to reflection, and others link it to the prophets gathered during the Night Journey.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to ask those whom He sent before him among the messengers: did God ever permit worship of anything besides Him? The commentators differ on who is being addressed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the reference is to believers among the People of the Book, the followers of the Torah and the Gospel, and that all messengers called to monotheism and forbade idolatry; they cite the variant reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd report that the reference is to the prophets gathered for the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the Night Journey in Jerusalem, whom he led in prayer, and that he was told to ask them but did not, because of the firmness of his certainty. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi take the question as a figure of speech meaning to examine the faiths and laws of the messengers, as one might say ask the land. Al-Razi holds that the question serves to affirm the Prophet's position and to rebuke the polytheists, since monotheism is common to all the prophets. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the verse implies an omitted phrase, namely the followers of the messengers. Most commentators agree that the question is rhetorical and negative, intended to establish against the idolaters that no messenger ever taught worship of other gods.

This passage tells how God sent Moses with His signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Moses declared that he was the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, but when he brought them the signs they laughed at them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the passage consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and compares the situation of the Quraysh with that of Pharaoh and his entourage, whose end was destruction. The commentators broadly agree that each sign was greater than the one before it, and that the punishments that struck the Egyptians, namely famine, the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood, were both a punishment for them and proofs for Moses, in the hope that they would turn back from disbelief. On the phrase 'O sorcerer' that they addressed to him, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and others see it as a respectful term meaning a learned man, since magic was then esteemed knowledge, while al-Hasan takes it as mockery. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the expression may be serious or derisive, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan argue that their breaking of the covenant after the punishment was lifted shows that their words were sincere. Commentators also differ on whether 'we will surely be guided' was a promise of faith or a simple statement. They also report Pharaoh's words about his kingdom and the rivers, his disparagement of Moses, Moses's replies, and variant readings of some words. All agree that Pharaoh misled his people, who obeyed him, and that God avenged Himself by drowning them, making them an example for those who came after.

This verse describes how Pharaoh and his chiefs reacted when Moses brought them his signs as proof of his mission: they immediately laughed and mocked them, without pausing to reflect. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the ridicule he faced from the leaders of Quraysh, since God's way with rebellious peoples is the same, and their end is destruction, as Pharaoh's was. The commentators agree that this laughter was derision. They also agree that the signs came one after another and each seemed greater than the one before, as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain, because people forget the earlier sign quickly. Al-Tabari understands the signs as proofs and arguments, while al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir include the nine signs and the plagues such as the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood. On the word 'magician' that the people used when addressing Moses after the punishment struck, al-Hasan takes it as mockery, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as respect, since magic was then a respected science. Al-Qurtubi also allows that it may have been a serious address. Finally, all report that the people broke their promise as soon as the punishment was lifted, and some note that the verse shows that seeing signs does not by itself bring faith.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of the signs Moses brought to Pharaoh and his court, each one clearer than the one before. Most agree that the punishment that struck them was the years of drought and loss of crops, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, and that its purpose was to make them turn back from their disbelief. Al-Tabari says this means returning to the oneness of God and obeying Him, and he quotes Qatada that turning back means repentance or remembrance.

Scholars differ on the phrase "greater than its sister." Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Shawkani hold that each sign was greater than the one before it, since people forgot the earlier sign when the next one came. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy argue that the signs were all equally great, and the phrase describes their greatness rather than ranking them. Al-Razi offers a third reading: each sign appears greater than the others to the one who looks at it.

The word "sorcerer" that the people used for Moses is explained by Ibn Abbas, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir as meaning a learned man, since magic was then a respected science. Al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj see it instead as mockery. Ibn Kathir adds that each time the people promised to believe, and then broke their word.

This verse reports that after the punishment God had sent because of their rejection of Moses, Pharaoh and his notables said to him: O magician, call upon your Lord for us, by the covenant He has made with you; if He removes the punishment from us, we will surely be guided. The commentators agree that these people made a conditional promise to believe and that, as soon as God lifted the punishment, they broke their word and persisted in their error. They differ on the meaning of the word magician. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take it as a title of respect meaning the learned man, since magic was then the knowledge of their scholars and was not a term of blame. Al-Hasan understood it as mockery, while al-Zajjaj explained that they had grown used to calling him this. Ibn Juzayy follows the latter view, whereas al-Zamakhshari argues that their promise was a pledge they intended to break, so the name and the promise do not contradict each other. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi offer other readings of the term. As for the covenant they invoke, the exegetes take it to mean prophethood, the granting of his supplication, the lifting of the punishment for those who are guided, or the pledge to believe and obey.

This verse describes what happened after God sent Moses to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs. They mocked and laughed at them, and each sign seemed greater than the one before, as the commentators note. When punishment struck, they asked Moses to pray to his Lord to lift it, and they promised to believe if it were removed. Once the punishment was lifted, they broke their word and persisted in disbelief. The commentators agree that the verb (yankuthun) means that they broke their covenant and betrayed it, and that they did not keep their word, which shows that their betrayal was repeated. On the phrase (O magician), opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it as a form of respect, since magic was then a respected knowledge and not a term of blame, while al-Hasan understands it as mockery. Al-Zamakhshari argues that their statement (we will surely be guided) was a promise they did not intend to keep, so calling Moses a magician does not contradict it. Al-Razi offers several other explanations. The commentators explain that the lifted punishment was among the signs: the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood, and that the trial aimed at bringing them back to the truth, which they did not achieve.

The verse recounts Pharaoh calling out to his people, boasting of his rule over Egypt and of the rivers flowing, as he puts it, beneath him, then asking them to see his greatness and comparing himself with Moses, whom he calls contemptible and unable to speak clearly. The commentators agree that Pharaoh relies on wealth and power to claim superiority, and that his words show arrogance and ignorance. They differ on the meaning of the kingship: al-Mawardi reports that according to Mujahid it refers to Alexandria, and al-Naqqash that it extended forty farsakhs, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take it as general authority over Egypt. On the rivers, Qatada speaks of gardens and streams flowing beneath his palace or before him, others of branches and canals of the Nile such as the Nahr al-Mulk, Damietta and Tinnis, al-Dahhak of the commanders marching under his banner, and others of his wealth. Al-Tabari reads "beneath me" as "before me in the gardens", while al-Zamakhshari reads it as mastery and control. As for "can hardly make himself clear", Qatada and al-Tabari take it as a speech impediment, others as the lingering effect of the coal Moses placed in his mouth as a child, and al-Razi holds that Pharaoh meant the force of his proof rather than his speech. The readings differ on the words for bracelets and angels, and the commentators explain that Pharaoh was seeking the marks of lordship. All agree that Pharaoh misled his people, who obeyed him out of their wickedness, and that their drowning made them a precedent and a lesson for later generations.

This verse records Pharaoh's speech to his people after listing his kingship and wealth: he claims to own Egypt and the rivers flowing beneath him, then declares himself better than the one he calls despised and hardly able to express himself. The commentators explain that mahin means weak and lowly, and that la yakadu yubin refers to the speech impediment of Moses, which they link to the ember he placed in his mouth as a child. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi read the particle am as meaning rather, or as an interrogative, while Sibawayh and al-Khalil take it as an implied equivalence, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss these grammatical readings at length. Ibn Kathir stresses that Pharaoh's claim is a lie, since God answered Moses' prayer to loosen the knot in his tongue. On the bracelets of gold, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that men raised to leadership were adorned with them, so Pharaoh asked for a visible sign of Moses' authority. As for the angels who accompany him, opinions differ: they walk with him according to Mujahid, follow one another according to Qatada, or support one another according to al-Suddi. All agree that Pharaoh deceived his people, who obeyed him because they were a wicked people.

The verse recounts Pharaoh's words to his people: he boasts of his kingship over Egypt and of the rivers flowing beneath him, then belittles Moses as a lowly man who can hardly express himself, and asks why gold bracelets were not cast upon him or why angels did not come with him in procession. The commentators agree that Pharaoh is using contempt and doubt to dismiss Moses' mission by worldly standards. The word mahin is explained as weak and contemptible, and the failure to speak clearly as a speech impediment. It was customary to adorn a man given authority with a gold bracelet and gold necklace, and Pharaoh asks for such a sign. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the common reading is asawira; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain the final ha as compensation for a dropped ya, while al-Zamakhshari notes several readings. On the meaning of angels coming in procession, Qatada and Ibn Kathir say they follow one another, Mujahid that they walk together, al-Sudi that they support one another, Ibn Abbas that they help Moses against his opponents, and al-Kalbi that they would be evidence of his truthfulness. Regarding the rivers, Qatada places them beneath his palace or in his gardens, al-Dahhak takes them to mean commanders serving under his banner, and most others identify them with the Nile. The shared conclusion is that Pharaoh measured prophethood by wealth and rank, and that God destroyed him and his corrupt people who obeyed him.

This verse describes how Pharaoh dealt with his people: he provoked them into levity and folly, and they obeyed him in rejecting Moses. It states that the reason for their obedience was that they were a people who had departed from obedience to God. The commentators agree that "istakhaffa" means that he stirred them up and drove them to answer his false call, and that "fasiqin" means those who depart from obedience to God. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that the word may mean that he made their minds light and ignorant, while Ibn al-A'rabi holds that he found them weak-minded and so made them foolish, and al-Farra' sees it as stirring them with desire so that they hastened after him. Al-Zamakhshari understands it as provoking them by speech. As for fisq, al-Kalbi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean disbelief, while others say simply that it means leaving the religion of God. Ibn 'Ashur explains that their obedience came from their recent idolatry, and that they returned to submission to Pharaoh for some small cause. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri make their wickedness the cause of their obedience, Pharaoh having made them his tool. All agree that the following phrase, "asafuna", means that they angered God, though there is a verbal difference between anger and displeasure. The commentators do not choose between these views but report them all.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of Pharaoh's people. After Pharaoh swayed them into rejecting Moses and they obeyed him, they provoked God through their disobedience, so God took vengeance on them and drowned them all together. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the verb 'aasafuna' means 'they angered us', and some add 'they incensed us' or 'they provoked our wrath'. Ibn 'Abbas also reports a second sense, that they grieved God's faithful servants such as the magicians and the Children of Israel. Because attributing anger to God raises a difficulty, al-Razi, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi read it as a will to punish, while al-Alusi also cites a view attributed to Imam al-Rida that God's friends are those who grieve and are pleased, and so their anger is ascribed to Him. Ibn 'Ashur sees a metaphor for their disobedience, since God is exempt from real grief. For 'salafan', the majority reading means 'forerunners', whereas Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'sulufan', the plural of 'salif'. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as 'varied desires'. All agree that God made them a precedent and a lesson for later generations, and some, like al-Baghawi, apply it to the disbelievers of this community. Ibn Sa'di stresses the warning against disobedience.

This verse says that God drowned Pharaoh and his people after they provoked His anger through disobedience and rejection of Moses, and that He made them a precedent that went before, and a lesson for those who came after. Readers differ on the word salafan. Most read it with a fatha on the sin and lam, as the plural of salif, meaning those who went before. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with two dammas, the plural of salif meaning a company that has passed. Al-Tabari also reports a reading sulafan, with a damma on the sin and a fatha on the lam, the plural of sulfa, meaning a group. All agree on the general sense that the salaf is what has gone before. For asafuna, Ibn Abbas and most exegetes explain it as they angered us or provoked our wrath. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur hold that when the word is applied to God it must be taken by its effect, namely punishment, rather than as a human emotion. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith describing an unexpected death as relief for the believer and regret for the unbeliever, and quotes Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz linking retribution with heedlessness. Mathalan is generally explained as a lesson or warning, and Ibn Ashur also notes it can mean a striking story that became a proverb. The commentators connect this verse to the close of the story of Moses and prepare for the discussion of Jesus and the idolaters.

The verse refers to the moment when the son of Maryam was cited as an example during a dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, and his people raised their voices in laughter and clamour. Most commentators, citing Ibn 'Abbas, tie the verse to the exchange in which Ibn al-Zib'ara, after the revelation "You and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell," argued that Christians worship the Messiah, Jews worship Uzayr, and angels are worshipped too, and that if these are in the Fire he would accept being there with his gods. The commentators agree that the word "yasiddun" means to shout, clamour or laugh, and they explain the scene as one of mocking triumph rather than sincere inquiry.

Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir record that the reading "yasuddun" (with a damma) is attributed to Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i, and means to turn away from the truth. Al-Tabari, al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i regard the two readings as synonyms, comparable to "ya'rishun" and "ya'rushun", whereas Abu 'Ubayda and Qutrub assign them different meanings. The question "Are our gods better, or is he?" is taken by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd to refer to Jesus, and by Qatada to refer to Muhammad. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the words "they only cited it to dispute" expose the argument as sophistry, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers the reference to Jesus the stronger view.

The following verses describe Jesus as a servant on whom Allah bestowed favour, a sign for the Children of Israel. On the phrase "and he is a sign of the Hour," the commentators differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean his descent before the Resurrection; al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean the Qur'an; Ibn Ishaq sees in his raising of the dead a proof of resurrection.

This verse records the objection of the Meccan polytheists when the son of Mary was cited as an example: are our gods better, or is he? Most commentators link it to an exchange between Ibn al-Zib'ara and the Prophet ﷺ. When the verse about 'you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell' was revealed, Ibn al-Zib'ara argued that Christians worship Jesus and Jews worship Uzayr, so if they are in the Fire, the idols may be too, and the polytheists rejoiced. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya transmit this context. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the verse concerns only idols, since 'ma' refers to non-rational beings, and that Jesus is not included. Scholars differ on the pronoun 'huwa': al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Atiyya take it to mean Jesus, whereas Qatada takes it to mean the Prophet ﷺ, a reading supported by Ibn Mas'ud's variant 'this'. The verb 'yasiddun' is read in two ways: with a kasra it means to clamour or laugh, as Ibn Abbas and al-Qurtubi say; with a damma it means to turn away. Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith that no people strays after guidance without being given to disputation. Regarding the next verse, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe Jesus as a sign for the Children of Israel. On the pronoun in 'he is indeed a sign of the Hour', most say it refers to Jesus and his descent before the Last Day, while Hasan and Qatada say it refers to the Qur'an.

This verse states that Jesus, son of Mary, is only a servant of God whom God blessed with prophethood and miracles, and made a sign and lesson for the Children of Israel, who could see in him God's power since he was created without a father. He is therefore not a god, as the Christians claimed. The words come within a dispute with the Meccan polytheists, who cited the worship of the Messiah, the angels and Uzayr by Christians to challenge the verse "You and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell." The commentators agree that the servant is Jesus and that "mathal" means a sign or an example. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the Quraysh aimed only at winning the argument rather than seeking the truth, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith of Abu Umama condemning disputation after guidance. For the phrase "If We willed, We would make angels among you on earth to succeed you," most exegetes take it to mean angels replacing humans in populating the earth, while Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean that they succeed one another. Readers differ on the verb "yasuddun": some relate the u-vowelled reading to turning away and the i-vowelled one to clamour, while al-Kisa'i holds the two readings to mean the same. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take the pronoun in "and it is indeed a sign of the Hour" to refer to Jesus, whose descent signals the Hour; al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to refer to the Quran. In every reading the verse denies Jesus divinity while affirming his servanthood and prophetic mission.

This verse shows that God's power has no limit: had He willed, He would have made angels on earth in your place, to succeed you. It is thus a reminder that angels are created servants, not deities. The commentators agree on the sense of replacement and succession, but differ on who succeeds whom. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada hold that the angels succeed one another, while al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir understand that they would succeed the children of Adam on earth. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy report that the meaning could be that God would bring forth angels from among you, as He brought forth 'Isa without a father, or would transform some of you into angels, an opinion that Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi attribute to some grammarians. Ibn 'Ashur judges the first sense to be the correct one, since the context shows that the angels' place in the higher worlds is not their own nature and does not make them divine, just as 'Isa's dignity did not make him divine. Al-Razi stresses the demonstration of God's power to create what He wills. Al-Sa'di sees the verse as a refutation of those who make the angels partners of God. Several commentators rely on this passage to reject the worship of angels and of 'Isa, referring to the episode of Ibn al-Zib'ara. None of the commentaries cited draws a legal ruling from this verse.

The verse says that, according to most commentators, the pronoun in « and indeed he » refers to Jesus, son of Mary, and that his descent at the end of time is a sign of the Hour's approach, so the listeners should have no doubt about it. The following instruction, to follow, is understood as following the guidance and law brought by the Prophet, which is the straight path leading to Paradise, while the devil is a clear enemy to be guarded against. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd explain the sign as the emergence and descent of Jesus before the Day of Resurrection, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite the many traditions describing his return as a just judge. Ibn 'Abbas read « la'alamun », meaning a sign, while the majority reading is « li'ilmun ». Al-Hasan, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, which makes known the Hour and its terrors; others take it to refer to the Prophet, the last of the messengers, or to Jesus's raising of the dead as proof of resurrection, as Ibn Ishaq reports. On the meaning of « do not doubt it », some read it as « do not deny it » and others as « do not be in doubt ». Al-Tabari prefers the kasra reading, and al-Zamakhshari notes a reading attributed to Ubayy, « li-dhikr », which supports the same sense. The commentators leave the reader to weigh these interpretations.

This verse tells believers not to let Satan turn them away from the path, since he is their clear enemy. Commentators read it as the closing warning of a passage about the Hour and the straight path. Al-Tabari explains that Satan diverts people from obedience to God toward other ways, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi cite as proof of his enmity that he caused Adam to be expelled from Paradise and stripped him of his garment of light. Al-Baghawi, al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti take the diversion to mean a turning away from the religion of God itself, whereas al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud also connect it to belief in the Hour or to following the Messenger. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi place the verse among the lines about the Hour and the straight path, and al-Qurtubi adds that the laws of all the prophets agree on monotheism and on the Hour, so one should not be deceived by Satan's whisperings or by the objections of disputants. Ibn Sa'di and al-Biqa'i stress that his hostility is constant, rooted in envy, and that he seeks out every weakness. Ibn Ashur notes that the prohibition is addressed to Satan himself, which implies that believers have the capacity to resist him. The commentators thus agree on Satan's manifest enmity and the need to guard against him, while differing on exactly what he diverts people from.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the coming of 'Isa, peace be upon him, to the Children of Israel with clear signs. They differ on what these "clear signs" are: Qatada says they are the Gospel, while Ibn 'Abbas says they are his miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and reporting hidden matters. As for wisdom, al-Suddi and most exegetes take it to mean prophethood, while Ibn 'Isa and others define it as knowledge of what leads to good and restrains from evil, and some take it to mean the Gospel itself. The phrase "some of what you differ about" is explained by Mujahid as the distortion of the Torah, by al-Tabari as rulings of the Torah, and by Ibn 'Isa as matters of religion rather than worldly affairs. Abu 'Ubayda claimed that "some" means "all" here, but al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and most scholars rejected this and held that the word cannot mean the whole. The verses that follow all call to fearing God, obeying the messenger and worshipping God alone, which is described as the straight path. As for the divided "factions," most commentators identify them as the Jews and Christians, while others, such as Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, understood them to be Christian groups that disagreed about the nature of 'Isa.

This verse is presented as words spoken by Jesus to the Children of Israel: God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him, and this is the straight path. Al-Tabari explains that the One who alone deserves to be singled out for worship is the Lord of Jesus and of his people alike, so He must be worshipped without any partner. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read in it that Jesus and his people are equally servants, needy of God and sharing in His worship, and that Jesus is a servant and not a god, which refutes the claims Christians made about him. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi take the verse as the end of Jesus's speech, while al-Alusi allows that it may instead be a divine affirmation confirming what Jesus said. The commentators generally agree that 'this' refers to monotheism together with adherence to the prescribed laws, and al-Tabari extends it to piety and obedience to the messenger. Al-Qurtubi concludes that worshipping God is the straight path and everything else is crooked. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the separate pronoun 'huwa' restricts lordship to God alone, and Ibn 'Ashur adds that placing 'my Lord' before 'your Lord' and the emphasis of 'inna' guard against exaggeration about Jesus.

The commentators explain that this verse means the rival factions disagreed about Jesus, son of Mary, after he was sent, each holding different views of him. Therefore God announces a punishment: the wayl, a valley in Hell, and then the torment of a painful day, for those who did wrong, meaning those who disbelieved and associated partners with God. The commentators differ on who these factions are. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi understood them to be the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who opposed one another. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil identified them as the three Christian groups, the Nestorians, the Jacobites and the Melkites, a view Ibn al-Jawzi also records. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the pronoun refers to the people Jesus was sent to. Al-Tabari holds that the disagreement concerns the Christians and those who differed about Jesus. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di hold that the disagreement covers anyone who refuses to affirm Jesus as a servant and messenger of God, while only the believers testified to his prophethood. Several exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, relate that the verse follows the Quraysh's dispute over Jesus. Al-Shinqiti explains that "wronged" here means disbelieved. The meaning of "from among them" is debated, and no commentator decides between the readings.

This verse says that these people are only waiting for the Hour to come upon them suddenly while they are unaware of it. The commentators explain that the Hour is certain to come and that its exact time is hidden, so that the warning is stronger, as al-Sam'ani notes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi agree that the addressees are heedless of it and will regret it when it arrives.

The scholars differ on who the pronoun "they" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the sects who disagreed about Jesus, while al-Qurtubi also reports the view that it means the Meccan polytheists who opposed the Prophet. Abu Hayyan, al-Jalalayn and al-Alusi take it to refer to Quraysh. Al-Alusi also notes that the verb "look at" can mean "await", used here with a mocking tone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that "suddenly" and "while they are unaware" are not redundant: the first describes the arrival, the second describes their heedlessness caused by worldly concerns, and al-Razi adds that they may recognise it when they see it. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as an answer to the question of when the painful day will come, the suddenness meaning that its time is unknown.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection, friends who were joined in disobedience to God will become enemies of one another, except the God-fearing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early commentators, citing Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, explain that every friendship not founded on God turns into enmity, while the friendship of the pious endures. Al-Mawardi gives two readings: the enmity may already exist in this world, as each leads the other to ruin, or it may appear in the Hereafter once they see the bad end. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi take the exception to mean those who avoid evil companions, since each of them finds benefit rather than harm in the other. Several scholars, including al-Sam'ani and al-Qurtubi, report that the verse was revealed about Umayya ibn Khalaf and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, though al-Qurtubi says its meaning is general. The following words, in which a caller addresses 'O My servants', are understood by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi as a promise that the believers will have no fear or grief, and will enter Paradise with their spouses. Commentators explain 'tuhbarun' as being made joyful, honoured or delighted, depending on the author. They then describe the golden dishes and cups, and the delights that satisfy desires and please the eyes, and they note that Paradise is an inheritance earned by good deeds.

This verse explains that friendships built on disobedience and disbelief will turn into enmity on the Day of Resurrection, except for the friendship of the God-fearing, whose love is rooted in God. The address that follows, "O My servants, no fear shall befall you this day, nor shall you grieve," is understood by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as containing an implied meaning: they are told they are safe because God is pleased with them, and they need not grieve for what they left in this world, since what lies ahead is better. They also cite a report from Ali about two believing friends and two disbelieving friends, in which each praises or condemns his friend according to the counsel he gave in this life.

The commentators agree that friendship founded on disbelief or disobedience turns to enmity, while the friendship of the pious endures, as Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada state. They differ on the nature of that enmity. Mujahid holds that it already exists in this world, since each adorned for the other what would destroy him, whereas Qatada holds that it appears in the hereafter after they see the bad outcome. Al-Razi offers a reasoned argument that affection based on a perishable cause fades, while affection based on an eternal cause, obedience to God, endures. Ibn Juzayy says that harm came to each friend through the other, while the pious gained benefit from one another.
