Readers differ over whether the final yā' in "yā 'ibād" is kept or dropped, and over the pronunciation of "lā khawf". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi report that the address is followed by God's words, "those who believed in Our signs and submitted," after which the disbelievers despair of this mercy. The verse is followed by a description of the delights of the people of Paradise.

This verse describes the believers admitted to Paradise, right after the text has said that every friendship not founded on God turns into enmity on the Day of Judgment, except the friendship of the God-fearing. The plain meaning, as most commentators explain it, is that God calls His servants who believed in His signs and submitted to Him, and they are told: enter Paradise, you and your spouses, you will be made joyful, that is, honoured, blessed and delighted. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that the word tuhbarun means being favoured or honoured, while Hasan al-Basri links it to joy in the heart and Mujahid to happiness visible on the face. Razi, Qurtubi and Shawkani repeat these meanings and add others, such as wonder or the pleasure of hearing. On the meaning of the spouses, Ibn Abbas and Qurtubi take them to be the believing wives of this world, others understand fellow believers or the houris, and Razi and Ibn Kathir cite reports describing the delights of Paradise. Grammatically, Zamakhshari, Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take the relative phrase as a description of the one addressed or as an apposition, while Zajjaj regards it as a qualifier. The commentators agree in distinguishing faith of the heart from outward submission, and they do not settle between the secondary readings.

The commentators explain that on the Day of Resurrection God addresses the believers: enter the Garden, you and your spouses, meaning you and those who resemble you in faith, including the companions and kin who shared your path. The word tuhbarun is understood as being made joyful and honoured, with the delight showing on the face. Ibn Abbas takes it to mean honoured in rank, al-Hasan joyful in the heart, Qatada blessed in body, Mujahid gladdened in sight, Ibn Abi Najih amazed at what is rare, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir delighted by hearing. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir stress the sense of grace and honour. On who the spouses are, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take them to be peers in obedience, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi take them to be believing wives of this world, and al-Qurtubi also reports the view that they are the houris. All agree that friendships built on disobedience turn into enmity on that Day, whereas the friendship of the pious endures because it rested on obeying God. The believers are told that no fear or sorrow will touch them. Several add that the Garden is inherited through deeds, yet entry into it is by God's grace alone, as Ibn Atiyya explains.

This verse describes the state of the people of Paradise once fear and sorrow have been removed from them: dishes of gold are passed around them, sihaf for food and akwab for drink, and in Paradise there is whatever the souls desire and whatever delights the eyes, and they will remain in it forever. The commentators agree that the sihaf are large dishes and that the akwab are drinking vessels without a handle or spout, as al-Sudi, Mujahid, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report. Most read the phrase as a general statement covering every pleasure of the soul and the eye, including food, drink, sights and dwellings, a point that al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress. For Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di, the word "forever" means that this bounty is lasting and never cut off. The readings differ over whether the pronoun appears in "ma tashtahihi"; the majority hold that both are sound and mean the same thing, a preference al-Tabari also favours. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti cite hadiths on the many dishes and varied foods granted even to the least honoured of the people of Paradise. Al-Qurtubi also discusses the prohibition of drinking from or eating off gold and silver vessels in this world, which he takes to be settled without disagreement. Al-Alusi adds that the direct address at the end is an honour given to the believers.

This verse says that the paradise promised to the believers is their inheritance, a reward for the good deeds they did in this world. The commentators read the inheritance as a figure of speech: each person has a place in paradise and one in hell, and the believer inherits the place the unbeliever would have had had he obeyed. Ibn 'Abbas, reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says this explicitly. Most exegetes, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, treat works as a cause rather than a price that obliges God, with divine grace at the root. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di make the same point, and Ibn al-Qayyim cites the hadith that no one enters paradise by his deeds alone.

This verse tells the people of Paradise that they will have abundant and varied fruit, from which they may eat as they wish; commentators understand it to include fresh and dried fruit, in addition to food and drink. Most exegetes, including al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, read the particle 'min' as partitive: they eat only part of the fruit, while the remainder is replaced, since the trees are always laden with fruit. They cite a hadith that whoever takes a fruit from Paradise will see two grow in its place. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Qasimi also accept that 'min' may be initial, and note the emphasis produced by placing the phrase first or the rhyme of the verse. Al-Alusi relates that the repeated mention of food in the Qur'an may console those who knew hardship in this world, and addresses ordinary people whose attention is limited to eating and drinking. Ibn 'Ashur sees the mention of fruit after food and drink as a sign of luxury and delight that all human natures enjoy alike. Al-Sha'rawi observes that the Arabs knew few fruits, which explains why fruit is singled out after food and drink.

This verse states that the criminals, meaning those who committed disbelief and sins against themselves, will remain forever in the punishment of Hell. The commentators explain that the punishment will never be lessened for them, and that they will be in despair. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand mublisun as despairing of any deliverance, while Qatada renders it as submissive and al-Sudi takes it to mean that their condition has changed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that God did not wrong them: they wronged themselves by worshipping other than Him and rejecting His oneness after proofs and messengers had come. Several exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, report that the damned call on the keeper Malik to ask their Lord to end their lives, and that Malik answers that they will remain. The scholars differ on how long the wait lasted: a thousand years according to Ibn Abbas, forty years according to Abdullah ibn Amr, and a hundred years according to Kab. Al-Zamakhshari notes that these periods alternate between silence of despair and cries for help. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi link the surrounding verses to the Quraysh and their plot against the Prophet, to which God responds with His own plan. Some passages also have several readings and grammatical analyses, without a clear preference being given among them.

This verse states that the wrongdoers, meaning the disbelievers and polytheists who wronged themselves in this life, will abide forever in the torment of Hell. Their punishment will not be lightened or reduced, and they will be dejected there, meaning despairing of any deliverance and silent with the silence of hopelessness. The commentators broadly agree that iblas means despair of all good and of God's mercy, though their wording differs: Qatada explains it as submission and loss of hope, as-Suddi as a change in their state, while Abu Hayyan and az-Zamakhshari add the notion of silence. Az-Zamakhshari and others note that there is no contradiction between this silence and the cries mentioned afterward, since these states follow one another over very long periods. According to Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Amr, the keeper of Hell, Malik, does not answer their call until a long interval has passed, with estimates ranging from forty years to a thousand years, and then tells them that they will remain there. The phrase 'We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers' is read by at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as meaning that God punishes them only for wronging themselves through disbelief and refusal to worship the one true God. Most exegetes hold that these verses are addressed first to the polytheists of Quraysh, while applying more broadly to anyone who merits this fate through disbelief.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of the criminals, meaning the disbelievers, who will remain forever in the punishment of Hell, which will not be lightened for them, and who will be despairing of any relief. Al-Tabari explains that "We did not wrong them" means God did not punish them unjustly, and "but they were the wrongdoers" means they wronged themselves through disbelief and denial of God's oneness. Ibn Kathir adds that this applies after the proof has been established and messengers sent. Ibn 'Ashur understands wrongdoing here as aggression against what God commanded, and "hum" as a separating pronoun that expresses restriction. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, also record the nominative reading "al-zalimun", where "hum" becomes the subject. All agree that the punishment is a just recompense. They differ on how long the wait was before the guardian Malik answered them: Ibn 'Abbas says a thousand years, Ibn 'Umar forty, Nawf a hundred, al-Suddi eighty, and the commentators do not settle the matter. Al-Razi and others note that khulud often denotes a long duration, while the majority take it as eternity for the disbelievers. Most link the verse to what follows, namely that God hears their secret talk and that His angels record it, a passage often understood as aimed at the Quraysh who plotted against the Prophet.

The damned call out to Malik, the keeper of Hell, asking him to beg their Lord to end their lives so they might finally find rest. He answers that they will remain in the punishment forever, with no escape and no death. The commentators agree that the request is a wish for death to escape the torment, and that the answer closes off every hope. They note that this cry does not contradict their despairing silence, since their state alternates between silent despair and outbursts of anguish. The commentators differ on how long they waited before receiving the reply: a thousand years according to Ibn Abbas, a hundred according to Nawf, forty according to Abdullah ibn Amr, and eighty according to others. Some readers recite the name as Malu by apocope; Ibn Abbas considered this unnecessary here, while Ibn Jinni saw in it a sign of their weakness. There is disagreement over who speaks the words that follow, God or an angel. All agree that the verse refers to the Qurayshites and that their dislike of the truth is the cause of their fate. Al-Razi and others hold that the verse concerns disbelievers rather than sinners. Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read the verse about their plotting as a reference to the Meccan scheme against the Prophet, which God will thwart.

This verse describes the people of the Fire who committed disbelief and sin. Their punishment is not lightened for them, and they are despairing within it, and God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves. They then call out to Malik, the keeper of the Fire, asking him to ask God to end their lives so that they may rest, and he answers that they will remain forever. The commentators agree that the answer came only after a long delay, but they differ on its length: Abdullah ibn Amr, al-Suddi and al-Baghawi give forty, eighty or a hundred years, while Ibn Abbas, in many transmissions, gives a thousand years. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the following phrase, 'We have brought you the truth, but most of you dislike the truth', is God's own rebuke to the damned, whereas al-Qurtubi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also allow that it is Malik's words or God's address to the Quraysh in this world. The scholars explain that the truth means the revelation and monotheism, and that 'most' may refer to the leaders or to all of them, depending on the view. Concerning the Quraysh who thought God did not hear their secret talk, the verse affirms that He hears it and that the angels record it, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Masud read the name in its shortened form, Ya Mal, which some accepted as fitting the weakness of the damned, while Ibn Abbas did not favour that reading.

The commentators explain that the verse poses a rhetorical question to the polytheists of Mecca: have they firmly resolved upon a scheme against the Prophet ﷺ and his message? God answers that He too has resolved upon a plan that will overturn their scheme. On the meaning of the verb abrama, the scholars differ. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it as a scheme for a scheme: if they plot evil, God plots against them in return. Qatada understands it as a firm resolve to reject the truth, which God answers with His own resolve to requite them on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Kalbi reads it as God decreeing their punishment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud follow the reading of a counter-scheme. Several authors, including Muqatil, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, relate the verse to the plot in the Assembly House, where the Quraysh chiefs planned to kill the Prophet, and al-Mawardi notes that God destroyed them at Badr. The next verse affirms that God hears what is secret and what is whispered, and that the angels record it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy cite a report about three men beneath the veils of the Ka'ba who doubted that God heard them. Modern commentaries such as Ibn Sa'di and the Tafsir al-Muyassar focus mainly on the final triumph of truth over falsehood.

This verse reports the assumption of the disbelievers that God does not hear what they hide within themselves or the private conversations they hold among themselves. God replies that He hears all of it and that His messengers, the guardian angels, are with them and record what they say and do. The commentators explain that the secret (sirr) is what a person says to himself or confides to another in a private place, and that the private talk (najwa) is what they say among themselves. Most of them connect the verse with the context of the plot against the Prophet ﷺ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others say the Quraysh had resolved on their scheme, and God answers that He will overturn it. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain the words as a counter-plan, while al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari note that God's plan answers theirs. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, reports that the verse was revealed about three men who spoke near the Kaaba doubting whether God heard them. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur mention this report while leaving its wording open to general application. Most exegetes note that the recording serves to preserve deeds for the day of reckoning, and Ibn Sa'di adds that knowing this should deter a person from wrongdoing.

God instructs His Messenger to say to the idolaters who claim that the angels are God's daughters: if the Most Merciful had a son, as you claim, then I would be the first to worship him. The commentators differ on the meaning. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take the conditional as a hypothetical argument used to refute the idolaters, and al-Tabari considers this the most sound reading. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and, in one report, Ibn Zayd read the particle as a negation, meaning that the Merciful has no son and that the Prophet is the first to affirm His oneness and reject such a claim. Others understand 'worshippers' as 'those who are indignant' or 'those who reject', citing pre-Islamic and Umayyad verse such as lines by al-Farazdaq. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as a rhetorical exaggeration that denies offspring by tying worship to an impossibility, a reading that Ibn Taymiyya and others criticised, while Ibn Kathir holds that a conditional does not imply that its condition is real. The passage closes with the glorification of God, Lord of the heavens, the earth and the Throne, and with the command to leave the disbelievers to their vain talk until the day they are promised. Some scholars hold this to be abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others take it as a non-abrogated warning.

In this verse God declares Himself free of everything the idolaters attribute to Him: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and the Lord of the Throne. The glorification follows the previous verse, which says that if the Merciful had a son, the speaker would be the first to worship him. The commentators agree that the verse denies any divine offspring and that it targets the claim of the polytheists that God has a son or partners. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada explain the glorification as a rejection of what they falsely say. As-Sa'di adds that the greatness of the creatures named, the heavens, the earth and the Throne, shows that the Lord has no need of a child. Ibn Kathir notes that the verse answers those who said the angels are God's daughters, and stresses that God's perfection excludes having a son or a wife. Az-Zamakhshari holds that the glorification shows that begetting belongs to the attributes of bodies. An-Nasafi argues that the Lord is not a body, since a body could not have created the world. Ar-Razi explains that begetting implies division, which is impossible for the necessarily existent God. Ibn 'Ashur considers that the phrase may be a remark by God or a continuation of the Prophet's words, and that it concludes the argument against divine offspring. Al-Qasimi observes that denying offspring follows from God being the Lord and Creator, unlike any creature. Ash-Shinqiti notes that similar verses express the same transcendence. Ash-Sha'rawi links the word subhan to God's absolute freedom from anything unfitting. The commentaries thus converge on an absolute glorification, and their differences concern mainly how they explain its basis.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to leave the disbelievers to their idle talk and play in this world until they meet the Day they were promised, which most commentators take to be the Day of Resurrection, though some say the Day of Badr, death, or punishment in this world. The verse belongs to a passage denying that God has offspring. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain the phrase 'He is God in the heaven and God on the earth' as meaning that He is worshipped in both, and that He is the Wise and All-Knowing in His management of creation. Al-Razi reads it as proof that God does not dwell in the heaven as a body occupies a place, and that His divinity does not require any localised presence. On the phrase 'If the Merciful had a son, I would be the first to worship him', the scholars differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and others read the particle 'in' as a negation, meaning that the Merciful has no son; Mujahid and Ibn Zayd keep the conditional sense, meaning that the speaker would be the first to worship God as one; al-Suddi takes it as a hypothetical with no reality behind it; al-Kisa'i, Ibn Qutayba and al-Farra' read 'al-'abidin' as 'the most indignant', that is, those who reject such an attribution. The commentators agree that the claims of the disbelievers are vain and ignorant, and that their idols have no intercession except for one who bears witness to the truth knowingly. Several hold the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others consider it unabrogated and a warning.

This verse declares that God alone is the one worshipped as God in heaven and on earth. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain that the inhabitants of the heavens and the faithful on earth worship Him and submit to Him, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di add that this divinity is His alone, while God Himself is above His throne. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Ashur take the two prepositional phrases as tied to the sense of worship contained in the divine name, which excludes any other deity, whether celestial, such as the angels, or earthly, such as idols. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi stress the sense of unity, and al-Qurtubi notes that some readers recited the name as Allah in both places. Regarding the closing words, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain them as God's wisdom in governing His creatures and His knowledge of their interests, whereas al-Razi and al-Shinqiti see in them an argument against divine filiation, since a wise and knowing being has no need of a child. Ibn Ashur adds that the verse answers the polytheists who gave a share of divinity to the angels and the idols.

This verse states that God is blessed and exalted, that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and all between them belongs to Him, that knowledge of the Hour is with Him alone, and that all people will be returned to Him to be judged by their deeds. Commentators read it as a continuation of praise that follows the declaration of God's transcendence above what the polytheists attribute to Him, including offspring.

Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, agree on the phrase "He is the God in the heaven and the God on the earth," explaining that He is worshipped in both. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya link the prepositional phrases to the notion of divinity itself. Al-Razi draws from this the point that God is not located in the heaven, since His divinity extends to both realms alike.

On the conditional sentence "If the Merciful had a son, I would be the first to worship Him," the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, treat it as a hypothetical whose consequence is rejected. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd read it as a negation, meaning there is no son of the Merciful. Some take the word for "those who are disdainful," a reading attributed to al-Kisa'i and Ibn Qutayba, though Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi consider it strained.

Regarding those invoked besides God, Qatada and Mujahid name the angels, Jesus and Uzayr, who are said to hold intercession, while others understand the idols. Ibn Juzayy and others stress that no one intercedes without God's permission. Most commentators take "except those who bear witness to the truth" to mean testimony to God's oneness made with knowledge.

The commentators explain that the verse denies that those worshipped besides God, such as idols, angels, and according to some, Jesus and Uzayr, have any power to intercede with God for anyone, and that intercession belongs to God alone, who grants it to whom He wills. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, agree that the exception covers those who bear witness to the truth, that is, who testify with knowledge and certainty that there is no god but God, and that these will receive intercession by God's permission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the worship in question as that directed at the angels, Jesus and Uzayr, making the exception continuous in their reading. Ibn Kathir, al-Samani and others read it as discontinuous, meaning that the deities have no such power, but the monotheist who bears witness to the truth is the one who benefits from intercession. Qatada and Mujahid hold that the angels, Jesus and Uzayr will intercede for those who bore witness to the truth, while al-Hasan takes this witness to be the testimony given in this world. Jurists, as al-Shawkani and al-Qurtubi report, derive from the verse that testimony must be based on knowledge. The verse follows the statement that the polytheists acknowledge God as their creator, and leads into the Prophet's complaint about his people and the command to forgive them and say peace; some scholars consider this forgiveness abrogated by the verses of fighting, while others do not.

The commentators explain that God tells His Prophet that if he asked the idolaters who created them, they would answer that it is God. He then marvels at how they still turn away from worshipping Him toward others, despite this admission. The next verse records the Prophet's complaint to his Lord that his people do not believe. On the reading of the word 'waqīlihi', the majority read it in the accusative, Ḥafṣ and Ḥamza in the genitive, and al-A'raj in the nominative. Al-Tabari holds that all these readings are sound and each has a meaning; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the Prophet's complaint, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari offer different grammatical analyses without choosing between them. On the phrase 'fa-anna yu'fakūn', all agree that it means how they are turned away. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verb is passive because they turned themselves away. The commentators link this admission to the argument that the one who alone creates deserves to be worshipped, and most do not elaborate further on this verse itself.

The commentators explain that this verse follows on from what precedes it and records the Prophet's complaint to his Lord about his people who called him a liar and refused to believe: 'My Lord, these are a people who do not believe.' Most hold that the pronoun in 'his saying' refers to the Prophet, and that the phrase expresses his grief at their disbelief and his turning to God, entrusting the matter to Him. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a complaint expressed in the form of a statement, and Ibn Kathir compares it with the verse, 'The Messenger will say: My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned.'

On recitation, there are three vocalisations. The accusative (nasb), read by most, has several explanations: coordination with 'their secret and their private talk', as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash held, coordination with the sense of 'knowledge of the Hour' as al-Zajjaj held, or an implied verb. The genitive (jarr), read by 'Asim and Hamza, is linked to 'the knowledge of the Hour'. The nominative (raf'), read by al-A'raj and others, is taken as a new beginning. Al-Tabari considers all three correct in meaning, whereas al-Zamakhshari prefers reading the genitive and accusative as an implied oath, with 'they are a people who do not believe' as the answer to the oath, which exalts the Prophet's supplication.

The commentators agree that God commands His Prophet to overlook the offence and to say 'peace', and then says 'they will soon know', which is taken as a threat. On the pardon, Qatada and others regard it as abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others treat it as a lasting command to patience and forbearance, as Ibn Sa'di emphasises in describing the Prophet's gentleness in the face of insult.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the harm and denial of his opponents and leave them, to say to them "salam", meaning a parting of ways rather than a greeting, and then to warn that they will soon know the outcome of their disbelief. The commentators present the verse as an answer to the Prophet's complaint to his Lord about his people who do not believe. Most agree that "safh" means turning away and not holding the wrong against them, and that "salam" here is a farewell. The disagreement concerns abrogation: Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil and Ibn 'Abbas, among others, hold that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Shinqiti reports that many scholars consider it not abrogated, since fighting has its proper place while pardoning the ignorant remains a noble quality. In recitation, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "ta'lamun" in the second person, while most read "ya'lamun" in the third. The exegetes also offer several senses of "salam": good in place of evil, forbearance, or simply a parting word. Al-Zamakhshari reads "wa qīlihi" as an oath sworn by the Prophet's speech, while others link it to "knowledge of the Hour" or to "their secrets and their private talk".
